paras: The lynching of Dennis McLellan took place in Kemper County, Mississippi, on July 15, 1882, when armed men took the Black youth from a deputy's guard on the road to the county jail at DeKalb and, it was supposed, hanged him. He had been accused of entering the bedroom of a Kemper County man's ten-year-old daughter the night before. The only source, the Meridian Observer, did not confirm his death but endorsed the lynching, and papers that reprinted it praised the act.

According to the Meridian Observer, on the night of Friday, July 14, someone entered the room of the ten-year-old daughter of R. G. King, whom the paper called "a most respectable citizen of Kemper county," and laid hands on her. The girl screamed and ran to her father, who searched with a light and found no one. The next morning suspicion fell on Dennis, a "negro boy" who had made fires and worked about the house until he was discharged the day before, after a track like his and a plank used to enter were found near the window.

King had Dennis arrested and taken before Oliver Brown, a justice of the peace, where, the Observer said, he admitted entering the room and "confessed the nefarious purpose he had in view." Brown committed him to jail, and late Saturday evening sent him toward DeKalb in the custody of a special deputy named Haile and a guard. On the way, "a number of armed citizens" took him from the guard, and the Observer wrote that "it is supposed" he "was at once strung up according to the code of Judge Lynch."
The coverage reports no body, inquest, arrests or official response, and none of the armed men was named.

The story survives only through reprints and summaries of the Meridian Observer, which carried an editorial line opposing "Lynch law" in general while holding that here "the protection of female virtue and the good of society fully justifies it." The Memphis Public Ledger printed the account on July 18 under the headline "Lynched and Served Right," and the Memphis Daily Appeal ran a shorter version among its Mississippi news on July 20.

Mississippi papers compressed the story further. The Panola Weekly Star of Sardis, spelling the name McClellan, called him "the brute," said that when the officers started with him to jail "he didn't get there," and added "Served him right!" The Jackson Weekly Clarion, on July 26, described "the lynching of a negro boy" and dropped the Observer's hedge, saying he "was at once strung up."

Whether McLellan was killed rests on supposition: the Observer's original wording, kept by both Memphis papers, said only that "it is supposed" he was hanged, while the Clarion's flat statement came from rewriting the same account. His surname appears as McLellan in the Ledger and Clarion and as McClellan in the Panola Weekly Star.

All four reports derive from one Meridian Observer account, which is not itself in the collection (A1, A2, A4, A5).
